Churn Analysis: Who Leaves, Why, and What Predicted It

A reading on measuring, decomposing and forecasting customer loss — and on the difference between a churn number and a churn model.

1. A Tuesday in Pune

At 9:40 on a Tuesday morning in March, Meera Iyer, VP of Growth at a mid-sized project-management SaaS company called Ledgerline, opened the board pre-read for Thursday's meeting and found a single red number on the cover slide: net revenue retention had fallen to 94%, down from 103% two quarters earlier. Ledgerline sold subscription software to construction and engineering firms across India and the Gulf, billed monthly at roughly ₹18,000 per seat-bundle, with about 2,100 paying accounts. The finance team had already drawn the obvious conclusion: churn was rising, and the board would want a plan by Thursday.

Meera's problem was that "churn is rising" was not yet a fact she could act on. It described a symptom, not a diagnosis. Some of that 94% was accounts that had explicitly cancelled after a bad renewal conversation. Some was accounts whose card payments had silently failed and never been retried. Some was accounts still logged in and using the product, just on a cheaper plan than last year. If Meera walked in with one number and one story, she risked authorizing the wrong fix — a discount campaign for people who were not price-sensitive, or a win-back email for accounts that had never really left. She needed to take the number apart before she could act on it, and she had two days to do it.

2. The Idea

Churn analysis is the discipline of measuring how many customers or how much revenue a company loses over a defined period, breaking that loss down by who left, when, and why, and using the resulting pattern to predict — and where possible prevent — future loss. The output is not a single percentage; it is a decomposition: a rate, sliced by cause, cohort and timing, attached to leading indicators that show up before the customer is actually gone.

The idea has no single inventor in the way a financial ratio might. Subscription businesses — insurance, publishing, telecom — tracked "lapse rates" for over a century using actuarial methods to price the risk of a policyholder leaving. What changed with the rise of SaaS and consumer subscription products in the 2000s and 2010s was the frequency and granularity: instead of an annual lapse report, product teams could see, weekly, exactly which cohort was leaving and which in-product behaviors preceded it. Firms such as Netflix and Salesforce, and later a wave of venture-backed SaaS companies, popularized cohort-based churn tracking as a routine operating metric, and an analytics vendor ecosystem — Mixpanel, Amplitude, ChartMogul, and peers — built tooling around exactly this decomposition through the 2010s.

The sentence Meera could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was this: "Our net retention dropped because voluntary churn among small accounts rose after we raised prices, and involuntary churn from failed payments has crept up independently — they need two different fixes, and I can show you the split."

3. How It Actually Works

The mechanics begin with a decision practitioners often skip past: what exactly counts as "churned," and over what window. A monthly subscriber who cancels is unambiguous. A usage-based enterprise account that quietly reduces seats from 40 to 25 is a partial churn, sometimes called contraction, and belongs in revenue churn even though the logo has not left. Meera's first step, therefore, was to fix definitions: logo churn (an account cancels entirely), revenue churn (₹ lost from cancellation and contraction, net of ₹ gained from expansion, over a period), and user churn (individual seats or end users who stop logging in, which can happen inside an account that has not itself cancelled).

The second step is to split churn by cause into two categories that behave completely differently and require completely different fixes: voluntary churn, where the customer makes an active decision to leave — cancels, downgrades, does not renew — and involuntary churn, where the customer's subscription lapses for a reason unrelated to their intent to keep using the product, overwhelmingly a failed payment: an expired card, insufficient funds, or a bank declining a recurring charge. Involuntary churn can be a third or more of total churn in markets with high card-decline rates, India among them, and it is fixable with billing engineering — retry logic, card-updater services, dunning emails — rather than with product or pricing changes.

The third step is cohorting: grouping customers by the month or week they started, and tracking what fraction of each cohort remains active in each subsequent period. This produces a retention curve, and churn analysis is, formally, the study of that curve's shape and slope. A curve that flattens after month three describes a healthy core of customers who found lasting value; a curve that keeps sliding toward zero describes a product nobody stays with, however many new users arrive at the top. Cohorting also isolates timing effects — a pricing change in one month should show up as a kink in the cohorts started after it, not before.

The fourth step, and the one most often left implicit, is building leading indicators — signals observable before cancellation that predict it. A leading indicator is not a cause; it is a correlate strong and early enough to act on. Login frequency dropping below a threshold, a key workflow (in Ledgerline's case, uploading a new project) not being touched in three weeks, a champion user leaving the account, or a support ticket about a competitor are all candidate leading indicators. The discipline here is testing each candidate against actual churned cohorts to confirm it precedes departure by enough lead time to intervene, rather than assuming a metric that correlates with churn in hindsight will predict it in advance.

Figure 1. The January cohort finds a stable floor near 62% by month four — the sign of a durable core. The June cohort, signed up after a pricing change, keeps eroding with no visible floor by month six, which is the pattern that should worry a board more than any single month's churn rate.

4. A Worked Example

Ledgerline's January cohort began with 180 new accounts. Meera pulled the raw counts still active at the end of each subsequent month: 180, 162, 148, 139, 133, 130, 128. Monthly logo churn is customers lost divided by customers at the start of that month. From month zero to month one: (180−162)/180 = 10.0%. From month one to month two: (162−148)/162 = 8.6%. From month two to three: (148−139)/148 = 6.1%. By month five to six, (130−128)/130 = 1.5%. The shape matters more than any one figure: churn is steepest early and decays toward a low, stable rate — the classic signature of a product where early users self-select out fast and the survivors stay a long time.

Revenue churn tells a related but distinct story. Average revenue per account was ₹18,000/month at signup. But 14 of the 52 accounts that left between months zero and three had downgraded once before cancelling, and 22 surviving accounts expanded seats, adding ₹9.4 lakh in monthly recurring revenue back into the cohort. Gross revenue churn for the quarter — cancellations plus downgrades, ignoring expansion — was ₹14.6 lakh against a cohort that started at ₹32.4 lakh MRR, or 45%. Net revenue churn, after subtracting the ₹9.4 lakh of expansion, was (₹14.6 lakh − ₹9.4 lakh)/₹32.4 lakh ≈ 16%. The gap — 45% versus 16% — is the entire argument for showing boards both: gross churn describes how leaky the bucket is; net churn describes whether expansion from survivors is currently disguising that leak.

Fixing card retries for a third of those — 5 accounts, roughly ₹90,000/month — moves net revenue churn from 16.0% to 9.3%, a larger swing than most pricing or feature interventions could deliver in the same quarter, and one that costs an engineering sprint rather than a discount.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Hold On To

Churn rate is a lagging summary; leading indicators are what you can act on

By the time an account has cancelled, the decision is already made — the analysis has diagnosed a death, not warned of an illness. A churn rate tells you how big the problem was last quarter. Only a validated leading indicator, tested against historical churners, tells you which live accounts are at risk now, with enough lead time to intervene.

Voluntary and involuntary churn are not "churn, two flavors" — they are two different problems

Treating a failed-card cancellation the same as a customer who hated the product and left on purpose routes an engineering fix (better retry logic) and a product fix (fix the disliked feature) into the same bucket, and neither team ends up owning the number.

Churn and retention are the same fact stated two ways, not two metrics to reconcile separately

Monthly retention of 92% and monthly churn of 8% describe one underlying curve. Teams sometimes report both as if agreement between them were a finding; it is arithmetic, not evidence.

A blended churn rate hides cohort effects that matter more than the average

An overall "6% monthly churn" can describe a stable product with one bad cohort dragging the average up, or a genuinely decaying product — and those require opposite responses. Always ask which cohorts are driving the blended number before acting on it.

Churn tells you who left and roughly when; it rarely tells you the true underlying reason unqualified

A cancellation survey answer ("too expensive") is a stated reason, not necessarily the real one — sometimes the real reason is that a champion left the company, or a competitor's feature shipped, and price was the socially easy answer to give a cancellation form.

Survivorship bias creeps into every churn model that uses only currently active accounts to define "healthy" behavior

If a model learns "healthy" usage patterns from accounts that happened to survive, it will mislabel new accounts that are early in a legitimately slower but eventually durable adoption curve, mistaking pace for risk.

Base rates matter more than model accuracy sounds

If true monthly churn is 5%, a model that predicts "will not churn" for everyone is already 95% accurate and useless; the right question is not overall accuracy but whether the model finds the true churners early enough, cheaply enough, to intervene.

Churn analysis cannot distinguish a product problem from a market problem on its own

Rising churn concurrent with a recession, a regulatory change in the customer's industry, or a funding freeze among a company's own customers can look identical in the data to a product regression; the analysis needs to be read alongside what is happening in the customer's world, not just the product's logs.

6. Consumer, B2B and Marketplace — and Early-Stage vs Large

In consumer subscription products — a fitness app, a streaming service — churn is high-volume, low-value per account, and largely self-serve: users cancel with two taps, so voluntary churn dominates and leading indicators are behavioral (session frequency, feature adoption in week one) rather than relational. In B2B, like Ledgerline, churn is lower-volume and higher-value, decided by a named buyer, often preceded by a renewal conversation and a champion who can be engaged directly; the leading indicator is as often organizational — a champion's job change, a budget freeze — as behavioral. In marketplaces, churn has two distinct sides that interact: a supply-side seller who leaves takes buyers with them, and a demand-side buyer who leaves reduces the marketplace's attractiveness to sellers, so churn analysis has to be done per side and then checked for the liquidity spiral one side's departure can trigger in the other.

Stage changes the picture too. An early-stage company with a few hundred customers cannot yet build a statistically reliable churn-prediction model — the sample is too small and too dominated by early-adopter idiosyncrasy — so the right early tool is qualitative: exit interviews on every cancellation, read closely rather than modeled. A large company with tens of thousands of accounts can and should build a proper predictive model, but faces the opposite risk: a small movement in the blended churn rate can hide sharply different stories across product lines or geographies, so segmentation discipline matters more than modeling sophistication once scale arrives.

7. Common Mistakes

Reporting one blended churn number to the board. Symptom: the number moves and nobody can explain which lever to pull. Underlying error: conflating voluntary and involuntary, and every cohort and segment, into one figure. Cheapest diagnostic: split the same number by cause and by cohort before the next meeting — if the story changes, the blended number was misleading.

Building a churn-prediction model before fixing definitions. Symptom: the model's precision looks good in testing but the business doesn't trust its flagged accounts. Underlying error: the training data mixed logo churn, seat contraction and involuntary lapses as one label. Cheapest diagnostic: ask the data science team, in plain language, exactly which of those three the model was trained to predict.

Treating a stated cancellation reason as the true cause. Symptom: the company repeatedly "fixes" pricing and churn doesn't move. Underlying error: taking survey answers at face value instead of cross-checking against usage data from before the cancellation. Cheapest diagnostic: for the last twenty cancellations, pull the actual product usage in the preceding six weeks and see whether it matches the stated reason.

Ignoring involuntary churn because it "isn't a product problem." Symptom: churn creeps up steadily with no obvious product or pricing cause. Underlying error: assuming all churn reflects customer dissatisfaction. Cheapest diagnostic: tag every churned account by whether the subscription lapsed through an active cancellation or a failed payment — if involuntary churn is a third or more, the fix is a billing engineer, not a product roadmap item.

8. What Good Looks Like

At a comparable company, Arjun Reddy, Head of Data at a Bengaluru HR-tech firm, faced a similar board question a year earlier. Rather than presenting one retention figure, he opened with a two-way split — voluntary versus involuntary — showing involuntary churn at 31% of the total and rising, in line with recurring-card failures after a central-bank mandate tightened payment authentication. He proposed, and got funded, a payment-retry and card-updater project costing about ₹6 lakh in engineering time, projected to recover roughly ₹40 lakh in annual recurring revenue — a return the board could evaluate on its own terms, distinct from any product change. Separately, he flagged that voluntary churn was concentrated in accounts that had never completed onboarding of a specific integration, and proposed a smaller, second experiment there. Two problems, two owners, two numbers to watch — not one churn slide and a vague mandate to "improve retention."

9. What Meera Decided

Meera walked into Thursday's meeting with the decomposition, not the headline. She showed that gross revenue churn had barely moved — the leak was roughly where it had been for a year — but expansion revenue from existing accounts had slowed after the March price increase, which was what had pulled net retention down to 94%. Separately, involuntary churn had drifted from 22% to 29% of total churn over two quarters, tracking a rise in failed UPI autopay renewals among smaller accounts. She recommended two independent workstreams: a billing-reliability project to recover the involuntary share, owned by engineering, and a closer look at whether the price increase had been mis-targeted at expansion-stage accounts, owned by product and sales together — deliberately not proposing to reverse the price increase until the two effects could be separated with another quarter of cohort data.

The reasoning she gave the board was the same one this reading has walked through: a churn number is an invitation to decompose, not a verdict to react to. What she planned to learn next was how to build early-warning scores from the leading indicators she had only informally noticed — the subject of resurrection and win-back analysis, and of the specific mechanics of involuntary churn in subscription billing, both of which take this decomposition further than a single quarter's board deck can.

  • Question 1. The next time you see a single churn percentage in a deck, what two splits would you ask for before trusting it — and what decision would each split change?
  • Question 2. For your own product, what is the earliest behavioral or organizational signal that reliably precedes a cancellation — and has anyone actually tested how early it fires, or is it merely assumed?

Vaani Connect: the three hundred and fifty-four

Lens for this case: churn analysis. Three hundred and fifty-four businesses stopped paying in January. The question is not how many left, but which of them chose to.

1. Monday morning, Indiranagar

On Monday, 16 February 2026, Sneha Varadarajan arrived at the Vaani Connect office on 100 Feet Road, Indiranagar, Bengaluru, at a quarter past eight, an hour before anyone else, because she wanted the conference room and the whiteboard to herself. She was Vice President of Product. On Friday, 20 February, she had to give the leadership team a single retention plan for the financial year beginning in April, and with it a claim on the one engineering squad the company could spare — eleven people, two quarters, roughly ₹1.6 crore of loaded cost.

On the whiteboard she wrote one number: 354. That was the count of paying businesses that had stopped paying Vaani Connect in January 2026. It was the highest monthly figure in the company's history, and it had grown in each of the previous five months. Underneath it she wrote the three sentences she had heard in the past fortnight, each from a colleague she respected, each proposing a different plan for the same squad.

2. Vaani Connect

Vaani Connect was founded in Chennai in 2019 and moved its head office to Bengaluru in 2022. It sold a cloud communications platform to small and medium Indian businesses: WhatsApp Business messaging through an official Meta partnership, a cloud IVR and call-tracking product, transactional and promotional SMS delivered through DLT-registered headers as TRAI requires, and a simple campaign builder that let a shop owner send a Diwali offer to eleven thousand customers from a browser.

Its customers were diagnostic labs in Coimbatore, coaching centres in Kota, real-estate brokers in Pune, gyms in Lucknow, tour operators in Kochi and a long tail of D2C brands selling on their own websites and on Meesho and Flipkart. By January 2026 there were 11,400 paying accounts on three plans — Starter at ₹1,499 a month, Growth at ₹4,999 and Pro at ₹14,999 — plus per-conversation charges passed through from Meta's pricing. Monthly recurring revenue stood at ₹7.2 crore, an annualised run rate of about ₹86 crore. Nearly all of it was collected by automated recurring debit: card e-mandates and UPI Autopay mandates registered through Razorpay.

The market was crowded and reputable. Gupshup and Exotel sold adjacent capabilities to larger firms; Zoho and Freshworks bundled messaging into suites that an Indian SMB could already be paying for; Interakt and a dozen smaller resellers competed for the same Starter customer at the same price. Vaani Connect had won by being easy: an account could be live, verified and sending within a working day.

The team was deliberately spread. Engineering sat in Bengaluru and Pune; Jonas Neumann led design from Berlin; Ishita Chakraborty, the company's only senior data scientist, worked from Toronto; Wei Ling Tan ran customer success from Singapore for the Asia-Pacific accounts; Arvind Pillai sold from New Jersey to Indian-diaspora businesses in North America; and the largest single account, Mawj Retail Group in Dubai, a sixty-branch home-furnishing chain, paid ₹41 lakh a year and had its own quarterly review.

3. The situation

The 354 was not, by itself, new information. Vaani Connect had always lost roughly three percent of its accounts a month, which the founders described to investors as "normal for SMB". What was new was the trend: gross account churn had risen from 2.68 percent in August to 3.11 percent in January, and monthly recurring revenue lost to churn had risen from ₹12.6 lakh to ₹17.3 lakh, even as the company kept adding accounts (Exhibit 1).

Sneha's first act had been to ask Ishita in Toronto for the cancellations split by how the account had ended. The answer came back at two in the morning India time, as Ishita's answers usually did. Of the 354 accounts lost in January, 226 had cancelled — clicked cancel, or written to support, or simply refused to renew when contacted. The other 128 had not cancelled anything. Their recurring debits had failed, four times over nine days, and the billing system had suspended them automatically. In August the second group had been 71 accounts. It was now 128, and it was growing faster than the first group.

Wei Ling, reading the same table from Singapore, made the point that mattered commercially: the failed-payment accounts were not small. Their median monthly spend was ₹5,400 against ₹3,900 for the accounts that actively cancelled, because higher-value accounts were more likely to be on Pro, and a Pro debit of ₹14,999 sat above the ₹15,000 threshold only occasionally but hit the additional-factor authentication rules and the twenty-four-hour pre-debit notification more often than a Starter debit did. Several of them, she said, had simply not seen the notification.

Jonas in Berlin had a different reading. He had spent three weeks watching session recordings of new accounts and had counted how many of them ever sent a second campaign. "The accounts that cancel in month four," he wrote in the shared document, "stopped using us in month one. We are not losing them in January. We lost them in October and have been billing them since."

4. The people

Sneha Varadarajan, VP Product, Bengaluru. Accountable for the retention plan and for the squad's allocation. She wants a recommendation she can defend line by line at Friday's meeting, and she is aware that whichever cause she names, she implicitly absolves the other two teams.

Ishita Chakraborty, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto. Owns the billing and product event tables. She wants the company to stop reporting a single churn number. Her private worry is that the classification itself is soft: an account that deliberately lets its UPI mandate lapse rather than clicking cancel is recorded as an involuntary loss, and she cannot yet tell how many of the 128 those are.

Wei Ling Tan, Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Runs a team of nine across Bengaluru and Singapore. She wants a save desk with authority to discount, because her team currently telephones cancelling customers with nothing to offer. Her team's quarterly bonus is tied to logo retention, which makes the fastest-acting option also the one that pays her people.

Jonas Neumann, Design Director, Berlin. Wants the squad pointed at first-week activation: a guided first campaign, a library of pre-approved Hindi, Tamil and Marathi message templates, and an end to the template-rejection loop that sends new users to support. He has been arguing this for three quarters and knows that it pays back slowly, which has cost him the argument twice before.

5. Exhibits

Of accounts suspended for failed payments, forty-one percent came back within sixty days, most of them after a support call or an e-mail, and many of them after several weeks of paying nothing while still, in their own minds, being customers. Ishita then split that group further, and the split carried the argument: accounts whose card simply declined returned at fifty-one percent, but accounts whose mandate had been revoked at the bank returned at sixteen percent. A revoked mandate, she noted drily, is a cancellation performed with the left hand.

Exhibit 3 answered the question Sneha had not thought to ask. The accounts that cancelled had stopped using the product long before they stopped paying: one user, one campaign in three weeks, and a history of rejected message templates. The accounts that failed payment looked, on every behavioural measure, like healthy customers. They were sending three thousand six hundred messages a month on the day the billing system switched them off.

6. The options

Option A — point the squad at payments. Smart retry scheduling that avoids salary-cycle dead zones, a card-updater integration, migration of Starter and Growth accounts from card e-mandates to UPI Autopay, pre-debit reminders in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu and Marathi sent over WhatsApp three days ahead, and a seven-day grace window in which the service keeps running. Ishita's estimate was that recovering half the card-decline losses would return about ₹5.8 lakh of monthly recurring revenue within two quarters. The cost is that the underlying reason the other 226 leave goes untouched for six months.

Option B — point the squad at the first fortnight. A guided first campaign, a library of message templates pre-approved by Meta in six languages, in-product template-rejection diagnostics, and an onboarding flow that a coaching-centre owner in Kota can complete without a support call. Jonas argues this raises the fourteen-day campaign rate from 38 percent to something near the retained population's 79 percent and therefore shrinks the cancelling cohort at source. It also cannot help anyone who signed up before April, and shows nothing in the numbers until the third quarter.

Option C — build a save desk. Fund six more people under Wei Ling, give them a daily at-risk list, and authorise discounts of up to twenty percent for six months. It acts on both populations immediately and requires no engineering. It costs roughly ₹1.1 crore a year in salary and discount, it trades revenue for logos, and it produces a retention number that nobody can decompose afterwards.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, describe in one sentence what actually changed at Vaani Connect between August and January. How does that description differ from "churn went from 2.7 percent to 3.1 percent"?

2. Exhibit 2 splits the payment-failure group into card declines and revoked mandates. What does the difference in return rates imply about how the 128 should be counted? Which of the two groups belongs with the 226?

3. Exhibit 3 shows the cancelling accounts going quiet weeks before they cancel. If you had to build one at-risk alert from this table, what would it fire on, and how many days of warning would it buy?

4. Which option should Sneha take to Friday's meeting, and what would she have to believe for each of the other two to be the better choice?

8. A note for the learner

Churn analysis begins by refusing the single number. "Three point one percent" is an average over two populations with different causes, different economics and different remedies, and averaging them hid a problem that had been growing for six months. The first discipline is the split between customers who decided to leave and customers whose payment stopped working — voluntary and involuntary churn. The second is to notice that the split is itself a judgement, not a fact: Exhibit 2 shows that a revoked mandate behaves like a cancellation, while a declined card behaves like an accident. Half the ostensibly involuntary loss at Vaani Connect is really voluntary loss wearing a billing error's clothes, and half is genuinely recoverable revenue.

The third discipline is the leading indicator. Exhibit 3 is the useful exhibit precisely because it is behavioural: cancelling accounts were down to one user and one campaign in three weeks, while suspended accounts were still sending 3,600 messages. That asymmetry gives Sneha two different early-warning systems — a usage-decay alert for the voluntary population, worth perhaps three weeks of notice, and a payment-health alert for the involuntary one, worth nine days. A save desk that calls both groups with the same script will fail with both.

A defensible path is to take Option A now and Option B next, and to say so in exactly that order. The reasoning is not that payments matter more than product; it is that the payments work is small, fast, uncontested, and attacks the part of the deterioration that Exhibit 1 shows to be actually growing — the payment-failure column grew eighty percent while cancellations grew fourteen percent. It recovers real revenue from customers who never wanted to leave, and it does so within the fiscal year. Option B is the more important work and the slower work; committing to it publicly for the following two quarters, with the fourteen-day campaign rate as its stated success metric, is what keeps it from being deferred a fourth time. Option C should be rejected as a primary plan, not because save desks are useless, but because a twenty percent discount applied to both populations would improve the logo number, degrade the revenue number, and destroy the very split that made this analysis possible. Sneha's strongest sentence on Friday is the one that separates the two problems before proposing anything: we have been reporting one metric for two diseases.

Churn Analysis: The Hazard Beneath the Curve

A near-expert treatment of customer loss as a hazard process — why flattening retention is usually sorting rather than improvement, why the churn event has to be invented in half of all products, and what separates a decomposition from a diagnosis.

1. Two Decisions, One Week Apart

On the afternoon of 6 November, Kavita Menon, Director of Retention at Rasa, sat in a Lower Parel conference room with a slide she did not believe. Rasa sold vernacular audio courses — spoken English, competitive-exam preparation, basic accountancy — to 312,000 paying subscribers across Maharashtra, Bihar and Andhra Pradesh at ₹399 a quarter. The slide, prepared for Series C diligence in January, showed monthly churn falling from 17.1% in the first month after purchase to 4.4% by the sixth, and carried the caption retention improving as product matures. Kavita had joined eighteen months earlier and knew something the caption did not admit: Rasa had shipped almost nothing to the post-onboarding experience in that window. The curve had bent anyway. She had a ₹3.2 crore budget approved for a save-offer engine — discounted renewals pushed to subscribers a model flagged as at-risk — and a growing suspicion that both the flattening curve and the save-offer plan rested on the same misreading.

Five days later and 980 kilometres south, Marek Dvořák, VP Product at Tessellate, was arguing with his own CFO. Tessellate sold AI document extraction — policy schedules, KYC packets, claim forms — to insurers and non-bank lenders on annual contracts with a minimum commitment and per-page overage. Thirty-eight contracts came up for renewal in the first quarter. The CFO's board pack showed 96% logo retention and 104% net revenue retention, both defensible, both computed from billing. Marek's own dashboard showed that nineteen accounts — half the renewal book — had processed fewer pages in October than in the same month a year earlier, several of them down by more than 70%. In a contractual business these accounts had not churned. In every economic sense that mattered to Marek, a third of his book was already dead and still paying. He needed a number he could take to the executive team, and no standard definition of churn produced one.

2. The Idea, and the Schools That Disagree About It

Churn analysis is the estimation and decomposition of the hazard of customer loss. Two definitions carry the whole subject. The hazard rate in period t, written h(t), is the probability that a customer who was still active at the end of period t−1 is lost during period t. The survival function S(t) is the product of the complements: S(t) = (1−h(1)) × (1−h(2)) × … × (1−h(t)). A retention curve is a plot of S(t). A churn rate quoted in a board deck is almost always an aggregate hazard for a single period, computed across a population whose composition is changing underneath it. Everything difficult about the subject follows from that last clause.

The intellectual history is older than software. Life insurers built lapse tables in the nineteenth century because a policy's value depends on how long the policyholder keeps paying, and reserving requires a lapse assumption alongside a mortality assumption; the actuarial vocabulary of hazard, survival and exposure is borrowed wholesale. Direct marketers in the 1980s faced the harder non-contractual version — a catalogue customer never announces departure — and the academic response, beginning with Schmittlein, Morrison and Colombo's Pareto/NBD in 1987 and continuing through Fader and Hardie's shifted-beta-geometric and BG/NBD models in the 2000s, treated customer death as a latent, unobservable state to be inferred from purchase timing. Telecom deregulation and number portability in the 1990s produced the third strand: large-scale individual-level churn prediction, the direct ancestor of every propensity model shipped by a SaaS analytics vendor today. The problem all three were invented to solve is the same one Marek has: a contract of unknown duration cannot be priced, reserved against, or acquired profitably without an estimate of how long it will last.

Four positions divide competent practitioners, and the disagreements are real rather than semantic.

The heterogeneity school, descended directly from the buy-till-you-die literature, holds that observed churn is mostly a mixture problem. It will sign the proposition that most of the decline in an aggregate hazard over cohort age is sorting — high-risk customers leaving first — rather than any change in individual behaviour, and that a two-parameter distribution fitted to aggregate cohort data forecasts retention as well as a hundred-feature model. It will not sign the proposition that individual-level scores should drive spending, because it regards individual outcomes as close to irreducibly random given a customer's latent propensity.

The predictive-intervention school holds that churn analysis earns its keep only through the actions it triggers: score every account, rank by risk, route the top decile to customer success or a save offer. It will sign that a well-calibrated model with adequate lead time is the highest-leverage retention asset a company owns. It will not sign that curve shape alone is actionable.

The uplift school is not a milder version of the second but its sharpest internal critic. It holds that propensity is the wrong estimand entirely: what matters is the incremental effect of treatment on an individual, which means four groups — persuadables, sure things, lost causes, and sleeping dogs whom the intervention itself pushes out. It will sign that a churn model's AUC is irrelevant evidence. It will not sign that treating the highest-risk decile is a sound default, because the highest-risk decile is disproportionately lost causes.

The diagnostic school, closest to jobs-to-be-done practice, holds that cause is never recoverable from telemetry and that the only reliable instrument is a structured switch interview conducted close to the decision. It will sign that a ranked list of churn "drivers" from a feature-importance chart is a category error. It will not sign that qualitative work scales to a forecast, and generally concedes the field to the statisticians when the question is how much revenue to reserve.

3. Mechanics in Depth

Start with the phenomenon that makes Kavita's slide misleading. Suppose a cohort contains two invisible segments: 60% of subscribers with a constant monthly hazard of 5%, and 40% with a constant monthly hazard of 35%. No individual's behaviour ever changes. In month one, the aggregate hazard is 0.6(0.05) + 0.4(0.35) = 17.0%. Survivors after month one are 0.57 and 0.26 respectively, a total of 83%, so the mix is now 68.7% low-risk. Month two's aggregate hazard is 0.687(0.05) + 0.313(0.35) = 14.4%. By month three the mix is 76.2/23.8 and the hazard is 12.1%; by month six it is below 9%. The curve flattens beautifully and the product has not improved by one basis point. This is the single most important second-order effect in the subject, and it is why the caption on Kavita's slide is a claim about Rasa's acquisition mix masquerading as a claim about Rasa's product.

Figure 1. Two segments with permanently constant hazards produce a smoothly decaying aggregate hazard purely because the high-risk segment is consumed first. Any product that acquires a heterogeneous mix will show a "maturing" retention curve whether or not it has improved. The gold line is what a dashboard reports; the two dashed lines are what is actually happening.

The formal treatment that captures this is the shifted-beta-geometric model, which assumes each customer has a fixed churn probability drawn from a beta distribution with parameters α and β. Its useful property is a closed-form recursion: the period-t retention rate among survivors is (β + t − 1)/(α + β + t − 1). With α = 0.8 and β = 2.5 — a plausible fit for a low-priced consumer subscription — the model produces the table below from two numbers. The point is not that the model is true; it is that a two-parameter description of heterogeneity reproduces the entire shape of a flattening curve without any story about product improvement, and therefore that any claim of improvement must be evidenced against this null.

The hazard falls by 60% across six months from a model in which no individual customer's propensity ever changes. Kavita's slide showed 17.1% falling to 4.4%; a fitted sBG null accounts for most of that movement, and the residual — not the raw decline — is the only part a product team can claim.

Three further mechanics are routinely left implicit. The first is the denominator. Blended churn is churned accounts over accounts at risk, and accounts at risk includes this month's new customers, who carry the highest hazard. A company adding 1,000 subscribers a month with a 30% first-month hazard on top of a 10,000-strong base at 4% reports (300 + 400)/11,000 = 6.4%. Cut acquisition to 300 a month and the same business reports (90 + 400)/10,300 = 4.8%. Churn "improves" by 160 basis points because marketing spend fell. Kavita has seen exactly this: Rasa throttled a low-quality affiliate channel in July, and the improvement visible from August is partly that.

The second is censoring. A cohort observed for four months cannot report a six-month number, and the common shortcut of dividing all-time churned customers by all-time acquired customers systematically understates loss because recent, largely un-churned cohorts sit in the denominator. The tell is that recent cohorts always look better than old ones, in every company, forever.

The third is the lifetime-value error that follows from ignoring heterogeneity. The familiar formula LTV = ARPU ÷ churn is the expected value of a geometric distribution and is correct only under a constant, homogeneous hazard. Take Rasa's numbers: ARPU of ₹1,200 per quarter, or roughly ₹400 a month, and a blended first-month hazard of 17%. The naive figure is ₹400 ÷ 0.17 = ₹2,353. Under the two-segment mixture that generated that same 17%, expected lifetime is 0.6(1/0.05) + 0.4(1/0.35) = 12.0 + 1.14 = 13.1 months, giving ₹5,257 — more than twice the naive number. Heterogeneity means the average customer's lifetime is dominated by the long-lived minority, and averaging the hazard before inverting it destroys exactly that information. Companies that set acquisition bids from the naive figure systematically underspend on channels that deliver low-hazard customers.

Finally, in non-contractual and usage-based products there is no loss event to observe, so it must be constructed. Marek's team must choose a dormancy rule — say, 45 days with volume below 20% of the account's trailing-90-day median — and every element of that rule is a policy choice with revenue consequences. A short window over-reports churn in accounts with quarterly processing cycles; a long one delays the alert past the point of usefulness. Serious practice adds competing risks: an account lost to a merger, to an internal build, to a competitor, and to budget freeze are four different events that are wrongly pooled into a single label, and pooling them is the reason most churn models produce uninterpretable feature importances.

Figure 2. Where the loss event is not observable, it is defined. Tessellate's dormancy rule fires up to eleven months before the contractual non-renewal that finance will eventually record, which is the entire value of constructing it — but the four competing risks behind dormancy have different base rates, different owners and radically different recovery economics.

4. When the Analysis Applies, and When It Misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: a dated, observable loss event exists. Rasa passes — a quarterly subscription either renews or does not, on a known date. Tessellate fails, and Marek's construction is therefore a measurement instrument whose thresholds must be validated against realised non-renewals, not assumed. Second: the population is stationary enough that past cohorts inform future ones. Rasa fails this badly; its channel mix shifted from organic app-store installs to affiliate-driven acquisition and back within a year, so cross-cohort comparison confounds product with source. Third: loss is reversible at a cost below the value recovered. Tessellate's in-house-build losses fail this; nothing Marek does after an insurer has hired four engineers will recover the account. Fourth: the unit of loss equals the unit of value. Rasa passes, since one subscriber is one revenue stream; Tessellate fails, because a retained logo on a minimum commitment may represent 12% of the revenue it did a year ago.

The analysis is actively misleading in three situations. Where churn is the intended outcome — a subscriber leaves Rasa's exam-prep course because they passed the exam — treating departure as failure inverts the product goal and funds retention features that trap satisfied customers. Where the business is growing very fast, denominator effects dominate genuine signal, and monthly churn is close to uninformative until cohorts are read separately. And where a regulatory or infrastructural change forces re-consent — India's e-mandate and additional-factor-authentication regime for recurring card payments is the canonical example — a lapse spike is a systems artefact, and a team that reads it as dissatisfaction will redesign a product that was never the problem.

5. Hard Edge Cases

Multi-product. When a customer drops one module and adds another, the account shows expansion in revenue and churn in the abandoned product, and companies choose which to report. The honest treatment is a per-product hazard alongside an account-level one; the common treatment is to let cross-sell mask module-level decay until the module is deprecated and the accounts leave together.

Two-sided. Churn on the concentrated side propagates. If the top 5% of sellers carry 40% of transactions, seller churn must be GMV-weighted, and the relevant analysis is conditional: what is buyer hazard given that their most-used seller left? Mature marketplaces model this as a coupled system and immature ones report two unrelated percentages.

Regulated. Insurance and lending carry grace periods, reinstatement rights and mandated communications that place a legal wrapper around the churn event; a policy in its 60-day grace window is neither active nor lapsed, and the choice of when to count it moves reported persistency by several points. Regulators also constrain the save offer itself — what may be discounted, to whom, and with what disclosure.

Hardware plus software. The device keeps working after the subscription stops, producing a zombie installed base that inflates active-device counts while revenue churns, and the replacement cycle imposes a hazard spike at three to five years that no in-product signal predicts.

AI-native. Two novelties. Usage is elastic in a way seat licences are not, so an account can decline 80% without any human deciding anything; and substitution is silent — a customer running a cheaper model behind the same workflow does not cancel, they simply stop sending the hard documents. The leading indicator worth building is task-mix drift, not volume.

The organisational seam. In every company past a few hundred customers, finance computes churn from billing, product from telemetry, and customer success from the renewal forecast, and the three disagree by five to fifteen points. What mature companies actually do — as distinct from what their metric dictionaries say — is nominate one number as the reported one and maintain a standing reconciliation of the differences, because the differences are themselves diagnostic. Companies that instead force a single definition lose the information in the gap.

6. Nine Things an Expert Sees That a Competent Practitioner Misses

A flattening curve is a claim about mix. The tell is that the flattening appears identically in cohorts from quarters when nothing shipped. The obvious reading — the product got better at keeping people — is wrong because sorting produces the same shape for free; the expert's first move is to fit a heterogeneity null and ask what the residual is.

Churn improves when acquisition slows. The tell is a churn improvement in the same month a paid channel was throttled or a promotional cohort finished washing through. The obvious reading is a retention win; the arithmetic reading is that the highest-hazard customers stopped arriving.

Save-offer results are mostly selection. The tell is a save programme reporting a 30% "save rate" with no holdout. The obvious reading is that the offer worked; the correct reading is that a large fraction of treated accounts would have stayed anyway, and some fraction were reminded of a subscription they had forgotten they had.

Stated reasons are a ranking of acceptable answers. The tell is that the share of cancellations citing price stays near 40% through a price cut and a price rise. Price is what people say when the true reason is embarrassing, diffuse, or organisational.

Involuntary churn has a voluntary component. The tell is that dunning recovery rates differ sharply by prior thirty-day usage — engaged accounts recover at 70%, dormant ones at 15%. A failed payment that no one bothers to fix is a cancellation conducted by inaction, and counting it as a billing problem overstates the recoverable pool.

Recent cohorts always look better. The tell is a slide where each successive cohort line is above the last, with the newest lines shortest. Right-censoring guarantees this pattern; only comparing cohorts at equal age is evidence.

The blended rate can move while every segment is flat. The tell is Simpson's paradox in the mix: enterprise and SMB hazards both unchanged, SMB share rising, blended churn up. Acting on the blend in that situation funds the wrong team.

Churn is a flow, not a state. The tell is that a resurrection programme reduces net loss while reported churn is unchanged, because the two are computed on different populations. Accounts that leave and return within two quarters are a meaningful share of consumer subscriptions — sometimes a fifth — and a model trained on a single-direction label cannot see them.

Lead time beats accuracy. The tell is a model with excellent discrimination whose average warning fires nine days before cancellation, when no intervention takes effect in nine days. An expert reads a churn model by its lead-time distribution and its cost-per-true-positive before looking at any accuracy figure at all.

7. How the Practice Differs by Product Type and Stage

Real differences first. In consumer subscriptions the hazard is front-loaded and behavioural; the informative window is days one to seven, the intervention is product rather than human, and the sample is large enough to fit heterogeneity models properly. In B2B and enterprise the hazard is concentrated at renewal dates, which makes it lumpy and largely unpredictable from usage alone; the dominant predictors are organisational — sponsor departure, budget cycle, acquisition of the customer — and with 140 accounts Tessellate can never build a statistically respectable model, which is precisely why a structured renewal review outperforms one. In platforms and marketplaces the analysis must be conditional and network-aware, as above. In hardware the physical replacement cycle imposes a hazard the software cannot see. In AI products the loss is continuous rather than discrete, which changes the measurement instrument but not the underlying hazard logic.

Where the difference is often asserted and is not real: the underlying mathematics is identical across all of these. Hazard, survival, censoring, competing risks and heterogeneity apply unchanged; what varies is the observability of the event and the size of the sample. Stage matters in exactly one way that is worth stating plainly. Below roughly 500 customers, no model is worth building and every cancellation should be read individually; between 500 and 5,000, cohort decomposition and a fitted heterogeneity null are the right tools; above that, individual-level uplift modelling begins to pay, and the binding constraint becomes segmentation discipline rather than statistical sophistication.

8. Three Worked Examples

The one that failed: Rasa's save-offer engine

Kavita ran the programme for one quarter before challenging it. The model flagged 10,000 subscribers as high-risk; all received a 40% renewal discount worth ₹160. Of the treated group, 9.4% churned against a 12.0% base rate in the unflagged population, and the team declared 260 subscribers saved. Kavita then insisted on a 2,000-subscriber randomised holdout inside the flagged group. Holdout churn came in at 10.1%, not 12.0%: the true incremental effect was 0.7 percentage points, or 70 saved subscribers, not 260. Cost was 10,000 × ₹160 = ₹16 lakh per quarter; the 70 saved subscribers, at ₹400 a month for a further 13 months, were worth ₹3.6 lakh. The programme destroyed roughly ₹12 lakh a quarter. The failure was not the model — its discrimination was fine — but the estimand: it ranked propensity where the decision required uplift. Recovery took two quarters. The team re-targeted on the modelled uplift decile rather than the risk decile, cut treated volume to 2,200, and replaced the discount with a content-unlock worth ₹0 in cash. Incremental saves fell to 48, but cash cost fell to near zero, and the programme moved from −₹12 lakh to +₹2.4 lakh per quarter.

Marek's dormancy instrument

Tessellate backtested the 45-day dormancy rule against the previous eight quarters of renewals. Of 62 accounts that had entered dormancy, 41 subsequently failed to renew or renewed below minimum — a positive predictive value of 66% — against a 12% base non-renewal rate, with a median lead time of 5.4 months. Applied to the current book, the rule flagged 19 of 38 renewals. Splitting by competing risk (Figure 2) left 7 winnable accounts worth ₹4.6 crore in annualised commitment against 12 where intervention was futile or the cause lay outside the product, which is a very different Q1 plan from "19 accounts at risk."

Vayu: hardware and the invisible cycle

Vayu sold connected air purifiers with a ₹690-per-quarter filter subscription. Reported subscription churn was a comfortable 3.1% a month until the third year, when it stepped to 7.8% with no product change. The cause was the device, not the service: units bought in the first big Delhi winter were reaching end of life, and customers replacing the appliance were not reliably re-subscribing. No in-product signal predicted it, because the predictor was the purchase date sitting in a warranty database nobody had joined to the analytics warehouse.

9. Failure Modes and Their Early Diagnostics

Reporting a blend across segments with different hazards. Early warning: the number moves and no team recognises the movement as theirs. Diagnostic question: if I hold segment mix constant at last year's weights, does the change survive? Cost of catching late: a quarter of roadmap spent on the wrong segment.

Optimising propensity instead of uplift. Early warning: a save programme with an impressive save rate and no holdout. Diagnostic question: what is the churn rate of untreated accounts with the same score? Cost of catching late: Rasa's ₹12 lakh a quarter, plus a trained expectation that discounts are the retention lever.

Defining the churn event by convenience. Early warning: finance and product quote numbers five points apart and both are "right". Diagnostic question: what event, with what date, is each number counting? Cost of catching late: a churn model trained on a pooled label, which cannot be debugged and must be rebuilt.

Reading stated reasons as causes. Early warning: repeated pricing interventions that do not move the curve. Diagnostic question: for the last thirty cancellations, does the six weeks of usage before departure corroborate the stated reason? Cost of catching late: a permanently lower price with unchanged retention.

Ignoring censoring in cohort comparisons. Early warning: every cohort chart shows improvement and the newest lines are the shortest. Diagnostic question: at equal age, is cohort N better than cohort N−6? Cost of catching late: a diligence process that discovers the improvement is an artefact.

10. Where Experts Genuinely Disagree

Is individual-level prediction worth doing at all? The heterogeneity camp's strongest case is empirical: simple aggregate models forecast cohort-level retention with errors of a few percent out of sample, while individual-level models with hundreds of features rarely beat a two-variable baseline on lift once deployed, and the residual randomness in a single customer's month is large relative to any signal. It would be wrong if intervention economics were sharply convex in individual accuracy — which they plausibly are in enterprise, where one account is worth ₹4 crore and a two-week warning genuinely changes the outcome.

Is involuntary churn a billing problem or a demand signal? The billing view rests on strong evidence: retry-logic and card-updater projects produce immediate, cleanly attributable recovery, often a third of apparent churn. The demand view rests on the recovery-rate asymmetry — if engaged accounts recover at 70% and dormant ones at 15%, most of the involuntary pool was already gone. It would be wrong if the usage decline were itself caused by the failed payment, which in products that suspend access on first decline it partly is.

Is net revenue retention a sufficient statistic? The revenue-architecture camp argues that above a certain contract value, logo counts are noise and NRR captures everything that matters, with the evidence being that public-market valuation multiples track NRR and almost nothing else. The counter-argument is that NRR can sit above 110% for years while the logo base erodes and the expansion comes from a handful of accounts — a concentration risk invisible in the ratio. It would be wrong if expansion were broadly distributed, which in most enterprise books it is not.

11. What Mastery Looks Like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask what the churn event is before asking what the rate is, and they treat the definition as a decision with owners rather than a convention. They reach for a heterogeneity null before celebrating a flattening curve, and they quote the residual rather than the raw improvement. They read a model by its lead-time distribution and its incremental effect on a holdout, and they will kill a programme with an impressive save rate and no control. And they hold the analysis loosely against the world outside the logs — a funding winter among a customer's customers, a payments regulation, a device replacement cycle — because they know that churn analysis locates and times a loss precisely and identifies its cause only weakly.

12. What They Decided

Kavita did not cancel the save-offer engine; she restructured it. She kept a permanent 20% holdout inside every treated segment, re-targeted on uplift, replaced cash discounts with non-cash unlocks, and rewrote the diligence slide to show cohort curves at equal age with the sBG null overlaid, describing the residual improvement — about 2.6 points at month six — as the product's actual contribution. Her reasoning was that a Series C investor who found the sorting artefact themselves would discount everything else in the deck.

Marek took the dormancy instrument and the competing-risks split to his executive team and asked for two things: a single reported churn definition owned by finance, with a standing reconciliation to his telemetry number, and a Q1 renewal plan scoped to the seven winnable accounts rather than all nineteen. He did not ask to change the 96% logo-retention figure, because it was correct; he asked that it never be shown without the volume-weighted number beside it.

  • Question 1. Rasa's flattening curve is largely a sorting artefact. Does that make the curve useless for forecasting, for valuation, and for product prioritisation — or useless for only some of the three?
  • Question 2. Marek's dormancy rule fires 5.4 months before non-renewal with a 66% positive predictive value. At what threshold of precision should he stop routing flagged accounts to a scarce customer-success team, and what would he need to measure to know?
  • Question 3. If involuntary churn recovers at 70% among engaged accounts and 15% among dormant ones, how much of the involuntary pool should a company count as genuinely recoverable — and who in the organisation should own that number?

13. Going Deeper

  • Retention curves and the PMF signal — the curve whose slope this page named; it supplies the flattening-floor test that tells you whether a durable core exists at all.
  • Resurrection and win-back — makes churn a flow rather than a state, and is where the uplift logic developed here pays best.
  • Subscription retention and involuntary churn — the billing mechanics behind the recovery-rate asymmetry that Section 10 leaves unresolved.
  • Constructing a funnel — the acquisition side of the denominator problem: mix changes upstream are what move blended churn downstream.
  • Reading drop-off — the within-session analogue of hazard, and the fastest route to the early-life churn that dominates consumer curves.
  • Defining activation (the aha moment) — the strongest known lever on first-period hazard, and the place where a leading indicator is actually causal.
  • Cohort analysis — the machinery that makes censoring visible and equal-age comparison possible.
  • Stickiness and natural frequency — sets the dormancy threshold: without a frequency baseline, every usage-decay rule is arbitrary.
  • Feature adoption analysis — supplies the candidate leading indicators and the discipline for testing which of them precede loss with usable lead time.

Bhor Fresh: four definitions of leaving

Lens for this case: churn analysis. Bhor Fresh has 2,64,000 subscriber households, four official churn rates, and a board call in thirty-six hours.

1. Sunday night, HSR Layout

On Sunday, 15 February 2026, at ten minutes to midnight, Aparna Menon was sitting at her dining table in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, with two laptops open and a printout of a board pre-read she had not sent. Her daughter's school bag was on the chair opposite. The pre-read was due at eleven the following morning, before a board sub-committee call at four, and it was supposed to answer one question that the lead investor's operating partner had asked in a three-line e-mail on Thursday: Why has customer acquisition cost payback moved from 4.1 months to 9.6 months while your reported retention has improved?

Aparna was Vice President of Product at Bhor Fresh. She had been in the job nineteen months. She had four documents in front of her, each produced by a colleague she trusted, and each containing a churn rate for January 2026. The four numbers were 2.9 percent, 6.4 percent, 8.1 percent and 11.7 percent. All four were monthly. All four were, in their own terms, correct.

The lead investor's term sheet for the Series D, signed as a non-binding indication on 22 January, carried a milestone: 2,80,000 active subscriber households on 31 March 2026. The definition of "active" in the term sheet was the one Bhor Fresh had used in its data room in November. It was the 2.9 percent one.

2. Company history

Bhor Fresh was founded in Pune in 2019 by Devang Shah and two classmates from the College of Engineering, Pune, on an observation any Indian household would recognise: the milk arrives before the newspaper, it arrives every day, and nobody thinks about it. They built a subscription: a household set a repeating morning basket — two packets of toned milk, curd on alternate days, brown bread on Tuesdays and Fridays, eggs, seasonal fruit — and found it outside the door before seven in the morning, seven days a week, including on Diwali.

By February 2026 the company served 2,64,000 households across Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, parts of Mumbai and Gurugram, took monthly revenue of about ₹58 crore, and had raised ₹410 crore across three rounds. Average revenue per household was ₹2,180 a month. The brand was built on cold-chain quality: its own chilling centres in Kolar and Ahmednagar, direct procurement from producer collectives, and a promise that the milk had been in a chiller within four hours of milking.

Two early decisions shaped everything that followed, and constrained what Aparna could propose on Monday.

The first was made in 2021. Rather than use third-party gig platforms for the last mile, Bhor Fresh built its own morning fleet: 5,600 delivery partners on fixed monthly retainers of ₹18,000 to ₹24,000, working a four-hour window from 4 a.m., each covering 90 to 140 doors inside a tight geographic cluster, out of 71 micro-hubs. The economics of that choice are entirely about density. A route with 120 doors costs almost exactly what a route with 70 doors costs. Every household that leaves a route makes every remaining household on it more expensive to serve, and the retainers are contracted in twelve-month blocks with sixty days' notice.

The second was made in October 2022. Bhor Fresh removed cash-on-delivery and per-order payment entirely and moved every household to a prepaid wallet with automatic top-up: the customer registered a UPI Autopay mandate or a card e-mandate, the wallet recharged by ₹1,000 or ₹2,000 whenever the balance fell below ₹300, and each morning's basket was debited from the wallet. The decision was made for cash-flow reasons and it worked: by 2026 the company held ₹47 crore of unspent customer wallet balances at any moment, which financed procurement. It also, without anyone intending it, made the word "active" ambiguous for the next four years. A household with ₹640 in its wallet and no delivery since November is, to the billing system, a customer in good standing.

3. The industry

The daily-essentials subscription category in India in 2026 was a strange, crowded place. Country Delight had built a national business on a similar promise. Reliance's Milkbasket operated in the north. BigBasket, now part of the Tata group, ran a subscription service alongside its main store. Against these sat the co-operatives that had defined Indian dairy for fifty years — Amul, Nandini in Karnataka, Mother Dairy in the north, Heritage in the Telugu states — whose pouches were available at every corner shop at prices Bhor Fresh could not match, and whose brand trust was absolute.

The more consequential competition was newer and did not look like competition at all. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — had by 2025 made a litre of milk available in eight to twelve minutes, at any hour, in every metro neighbourhood Bhor Fresh served. Subscription's original argument was convenience and certainty; ten-minute delivery answered convenience directly. Bhor Fresh's internal surveys in Bengaluru showed 61 percent of its lapsed households reporting that they now bought milk "as needed" rather than from a competing subscription. Nobody had won those households; they had simply stopped being subscribers.

Regulation touched the business at three points. FSSAI rules governed cold-chain handling, labelling and the claims the company could make about its paneer and ghee. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, whose rules had been phasing in through 2025 and 2026, bore directly on a business that knew when 2,64,000 families were away from home — the consent notices had been rewritten twice, and a January revision had quietly narrowed what the growth team could use for win-back messaging. And the wallet itself sat inside the NPCI and RBI framework for recurring payments: mandate registration, the twenty-four-hour pre-debit notification, additional-factor authentication above the prescribed threshold, and issuer-side controls that changed from time to time without Bhor Fresh being consulted.

The company's exposure beyond India was small but politically large. Rajeev Trivedi's team in New Jersey sold ghee, paneer and ready-to-cook items to Indian grocery chains in the United States, a business of ₹64 crore a year at good margins. And a franchise pilot in Dubai, run with Rimaal Foods, a local distributor serving expatriate households in Al Nahda and Business Bay, had been live since August 2025 with 4,100 subscribers. Rimaal had recently asked for six-month exclusivity across the Emirates in exchange for committing to 20,000 households by December 2026.

4. The situation in detail

The story Aparna could reconstruct by Sunday night ran as follows.

In January 2025 the growth team, under pressure to show household growth ahead of the Series D, launched a "First Month at ₹1" offer across Bengaluru and Hyderabad, promoted on Meta and Google and through society WhatsApp groups. It worked spectacularly. Sign-ups tripled. Between January and June 2025 the company added 96,000 households, the fastest six months in its history, and the blended acquisition cost fell to ₹720 because the offer did so much of the selling.

In March 2025, responding to the single largest category of support complaints — customers going out of town and being charged for milk left at an empty door — the team shipped a pause feature. A household could pause deliveries for up to thirty days from the app in two taps. It was a good feature. Complaint volume fell 38 percent in six weeks. It also had an effect nobody modelled: a paused household kept its wallet balance, kept its subscription record, and continued to count as active on every dashboard in the company. The measured monthly churn rate fell from 4.2 percent to 2.9 percent in the two months after launch, and the improvement was reported to the board in April as evidence that the retention work was landing.

In June 2025 Ipsita Bose, the principal data scientist in Toronto, circulated a memo arguing that the company's churn number was measuring the wrong event. She proposed a delivery-based definition: a household is churned if it has received no delivery for fourteen consecutive days. Under that definition, she showed, the January 2025 cohort had retained 41 percent at month six, not the 78 percent on the dashboard. The memo was discussed, acknowledged as interesting, and not adopted, on the reasonable ground that changing the definition three months before a fundraise would look like changing the definition three months before a fundraise.

In August 2025 the wallet auto-recharge success rate began to fall. Issuer-side controls on recurring mandates had tightened across the industry; some customers' pre-debit notifications went unanswered; a proportion of mandates were revoked at the bank by customers who had simply forgotten what the debit was for. The effect was invisible for weeks, because a household with a failed recharge does not complain — it simply stops receiving deliveries once its balance runs out, and the app shows a polite banner it may never open. Harsh Vardhan Pathak's hub managers in Pune noticed only that some routes had fewer doors.

September and October brought Ganesh Chaturthi, Navratri and Diwali, and with them the largest travel season of the Indian year. Pause usage rose to 31 percent of households in a single week in October. The resume rate — the share of paused households that had a delivery within fourteen days of the pause ending — was 74 percent in March and 58 percent in October. Nobody was watching the resume rate; it did not appear on any dashboard until Ipsita built one in January.

In November, after a rise in procurement prices, Bhor Fresh increased the price of toned milk by ₹3 a litre. In the same month, quietly, Harsh's team stopped serving 130 apartment societies whose route density had fallen below the viability line. The households in those societies were sent an e-mail and a ₹500 wallet refund. Nobody recorded them separately; they entered the churn numbers as ordinary losses, and they had been in the acquisition numbers nine months earlier as ₹1 trial customers.

What has since turned out to be wrong is not one thing but a sequence. The retention improvement of 2025 was substantially an artefact of the pause feature. The acquisition efficiency of 2025 was substantially an artefact of a ₹1 offer whose cohorts were counted from the day they signed up. And the 2,80,000-household milestone in the term sheet is written in a definition that the company's own data scientist has argued, in writing, since June, does not mean what it appears to mean.

8. The options as Aparna currently sees them

Option A — treat it as an involuntary-churn problem. Rebuild the wallet: lower the auto-recharge trigger, migrate card mandates to UPI Autopay, add a three-day delivery grace window on a zero balance, send pre-debit reminders over WhatsApp in Kannada, Marathi, Telugu and Hindi, and stop expiring mandates at sixty days. Cost roughly ₹2.4 crore and one squad for two quarters. Rukmini supports it, it is uncontroversial, and Exhibit 4 gives it a number to aim at. It also rests on a table that is missing 28 percent of the payment base, and it assumes that a household at zero balance wanted to be recharged.

Option B — treat it as a product problem. Rebuild the pause-and-resume journey, add a scheduled auto-resume, offer a reduced festival basket instead of a full pause, and fix the substitution and quality-credit flows Grace's tickets point to. Cost roughly ₹3.1 crore and the same squad, with nothing visible before June. Lukas and Grace support it for different reasons, which is either corroboration or two people reading the same ambiguity in their own favour.

Option C — treat it as a density problem. Accept Exhibit 6, exit the remaining sub-60 routes and the thinner 60-to-89 band, concentrate the fleet, and buy density back with society-level acquisition. It protects contribution immediately and it reduces the household count by perhaps 18,000 before 31 March, which is the one thing the term sheet cannot absorb.

Each option names a cause. None of them has been tested against the others, because no two of the exhibits are constructed on the same population, and the bridge between Exhibits 2 and 3 does not exist. It is also possible that the three causes are not competing at all — that a household whose milk was bad in May pauses in June, whose mandate lapses in August because there is nothing to debit, and whose route thins in November because six neighbours did the same, is a single household appearing in all three exhibits as three different kinds of loss.
